content.text: Admissions is the first contact between new families and the school community. It sets the tone for the partnership between home and school. It builds trust, openness and a shared commitment to student success. A well-designed admissions policy makes sure that:
content.title: Purpose of Admissions Policy

items: Every child who can benefit from our Cambridge international education has fair and equitable access to enrollment
Families understand our educational philosophy, expectations, and support systems
The school keeps suitable class sizes and teacher-student ratios
Students are placed where they can do well academically, socially and emotionally
The school follows Indonesian regulations and also meets international accreditation standards

content.text: Our admissions practices directly support the school's mission: to develop learners who are globally competent and guided by strong values. The process is designed to find students who will:
content.title: Alignment with School Mission and SLOs

items: Benefit from the Cambridge curriculum combined with Indonesian national subjects
Make a positive contribution to our inclusive, multicultural learning community
Develop the six Schoolwide Learner Outcomes (SLOs): Academic Excellence, Communication, Global Competence, Ethical Leadership, Innovation & Creativity, and Wellbeing
Show the values of Profil Pelajar Pancasila and also develop international-mindedness

content.text: Eduversal Partner Schools are committed to admitting students with different backgrounds, abilities and experiences. Our admissions policy:
content.title: Commitment to Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion

items: Does NOT discriminate based on religion, ethnicity, gender, socioeconomic status, or learning differences
DOES look at each applicant as a whole person, because academic potential shows itself in different ways
Provides reasonable accommodations for students with Special Educational Needs (SEN)
Supports English as an Additional Language (EAL) learners through placement that matches their needs and step-by-step teaching support (scaffolded instruction)
Offers scholarships and financial aid where available, to make sure students come from different economic backgrounds

content.text: We keep high academic standards in line with Cambridge International education. At the same time, we recognize that:
content.title: Balance Between Academic Standards and Access

items: Entry assessments are diagnostic tools (to understand needs), not gatekeeping tools (to keep students out)
Students develop at different speeds and come from different educational backgrounds
A student's level of English (EAL proficiency) should not be confused with academic ability
With the right support, most students can succeed in an international curriculum
Our Multi-Tiered System of Support (MTSS) lets teachers adapt their teaching (differentiated instruction) for different learners (see Section 8)

content.text: Open Enrollment Philosophy Eduversal Partner Schools aim to be open to all students while keeping the quality of education high:

items: We welcome students from different educational backgrounds. These include Indonesian national schools, international schools, homeschool programs and schools overseas
We do not require entrance examinations for admission. We use placement assessments to place students at the right level
We accept mid-year transfers when there is space, and we give suitable support for the transition

content.text: However, schools must be open and clear about:

items: Current capacity (places available) and realistic waiting times
The academic demands of the Cambridge curriculum
The support services available and their limits
The expected language level and the language support provided

Year 3: 7-8 years old
Year 4: 8-9 years old
Year 5: 9-10 years old
Year 6: 10-11 years old
Year 7: 11-12 years old
Year 8: 12-13 years old
Year 9: 13-14 years old
Year 10: 14-15 years old

Age requirements follow the Permendikbudristek regulations on PPDB (Penerimaan Peserta Didik Baru, the state new-student admission system). Academic Readiness Criteria Schools do not use fixed cut-off scores. Instead, they look at the whole student to judge readiness: For Primary Students:

items: Basic literacy and numeracy suitable for the previous grade level
Social-emotional readiness for classroom routines
Previous school reports (if available)
Parent input on how the child likes to learn and what they find difficult
Review of transcripts and academic records from the previous school
Placement assessments in English and Mathematics
Subject-specific screening for science courses (Year 9 and above)
Interview with subject leaders or Principal

content.text: Important Principle: Past academic struggles should NOT automatically disqualify a student. Schools should consider:

items: Reasons for earlier difficulties (e.g., language barriers, too little support, family circumstances)
Evidence of growth mindset and willingness to work hard
Whether the school has suitable interventions available

content.text: EAL Proficiency Considerations The school assesses English level, but does NOT use it as a barrier to admission:

items.text: Students are placed based on CEFR (Common European Framework of Reference) levels:
items: Primary: A1 (beginner) to B1 (intermediate)
Lower Secondary: A2 (elementary) to B2 (upper intermediate)
IGCSE: B1 (intermediate) to C1 (advanced)
A Level: B2 (upper intermediate) to C1 (advanced)

items.text: Schools provide tiered EAL support (see Section 8.4):
items: Tier 1: Adapted teaching (differentiation) and step-by-step support (scaffolding) in class
Tier 2: Small-group sessions outside the main class (3-5 students)
Tier 3: Intensive 1-on-1 language support
EAL students may need extra time (1-3 years) to reach the academic English expected at their grade level
Families are told about realistic timelines for English fluency
Schools should NOT promise immediate fluency or refuse admission just because of limited English

content.text: Assessment Note: Use tasks with less language when you assess EAL learners' subject knowledge in mathematics or science. Do not confuse a student's English level with their thinking ability. SEN and Learning Support Access Eduversal Partner Schools are committed to inclusive education, as far as their capacity allows: Admission Considerations for SEN Students:

items: Students with documented learning differences (e.g., dyslexia, ADHD, ASD) are welcome
Admission decisions depend on whether the school can reasonably meet the child's needs
Parents must provide complete documentation (psychological assessments, IEPs from previous schools)
A meeting between parents, Principal, and Learning Support Coordinator is required before final enrollment
Extended time on assessments
Modified assignments and differentiated materials
Assistive technology (text-to-speech, graphic organizers)
Preferential seating and movement breaks
Access to counseling and social-emotional support
1-on-1 teaching assistants (shadow teachers), unless the family pays for them from outside the school
Curriculum changes that work against Cambridge assessment objectives
Specialist therapy services (e.g., speech therapy, occupational therapy) beyond basic school counseling

content.text: Honesty is Essential: If the school does not have the capacity to support a student's needs, the ethical choice is to recommend another placement. This is better than admitting the student and giving poor support. For Cambridge Access Arrangements (exam accommodations), see 10.6 and 8.6.

content.text: Non-Discrimination Policy Eduversal Partner Schools clearly prohibit discrimination in admissions based on:

items: Religion (schools welcome Muslim, Christian, Hindu, Buddhist, and other faiths)
Ethnicity or national origin

Disability or learning differences

content.text: Islamic Boarding Schools: These schools include Islamic values and practices in school life. They may still enroll non-Muslim students who respect and take part in the school community's Islamic ethos. Compliance: This policy follows Indonesian Constitution Article 31 (right to education) and Law No. 20/2003 on the National Education System. Sibling Priority and Legacy Considerations Many schools give enrollment priority to:

items: Siblings of currently enrolled students
Children of alumni
Children of school staff
Makes family life easier (shared schedules, carpooling)
Strengthens school community cohesion
Gives continuity to families already committed to the school culture
Sibling priority does NOT mean automatic admission without assessment
If a sibling has very different learning needs that are beyond the school's capacity, admission may not be appropriate
Schools should be honest with families rather than admit students they cannot support
The full tuition and fee schedule must be published on the school website and in admissions materials
Breakdown of costs: tuition, enrollment fee, uniform, textbooks, trips, boarding (if applicable)
Payment plans and accepted payment methods
Schools may offer merit-based or need-based scholarships (if Yayasan permits)
Scholarship criteria must be clear to families and applied the same way to everyone
Process to check financial need (e.g., parent income documentation)
Scholarship recipients must keep satisfactory academic progress and behavior

content.text: Important: Do NOT promise financial aid during admissions if funding is uncertain. Set realistic expectations about available support.

content.text: Placement assessments are for diagnosis (understanding needs), NOT for selection:
content.title: Purpose of Placement Tests

items: Decide the right year level for the student (especially mid-year or transfer students)
Identify EAL support needs and CEFR level
Show strengths and areas that need extra support
Help plan Tier 2 or Tier 3 interventions (see Section 8.2)
Collect baseline data to monitor progress

content.text: Schools should tell families clearly: "These assessments help us understand your child's current learning profile so we can provide the right support. They are NOT tests to pass or fail."

Components of EAL Assessment:

1. Reading Comprehension:

content.title: English Language Assessment — Skill Weightings and Descriptors
rows: Fluency, pronunciation, vocabulary range, grammatical accuracy, interaction ability
Understanding of spoken language (conversations, lectures, audio passages); ability to find main ideas and details
Understanding of written texts (find main ideas, infer meaning, understand vocabulary in context)
Sentence structure, grammar, spelling, organization, clarity of expression

items: Age-appropriate passages with comprehension questions
Assess literal understanding, inference, vocabulary
content.title: English Language Assessment

items: Writing sample based on a prompt (e.g., "Describe your favorite holiday" for primary; "Explain a book you've read" for secondary)
Check sentence structure, grammar, spelling, organization
Conversational interview (part of student interview)
Assess fluency, pronunciation, vocabulary range
Short audio passage with follow-up questions
Evaluate comprehension of spoken English

content.title: CEFR Placement Rubric — Can Do Descriptors
rows: Understand and use familiar everyday expressions; introduce self and others; ask and answer simple questions about personal details
Communicate in simple, routine tasks; describe background, immediate environment, and matters of immediate need in simple terms
Understand main points of clear standard input; deal with most situations while traveling; produce simple connected text on familiar topics
Understand complex text on concrete and abstract topics; interact with fluency and spontaneity; produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects
Understand demanding, longer texts and recognize implicit meaning; express ideas fluently and spontaneously; produce well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects
Understand virtually everything heard or read; express self spontaneously, very fluently, and precisely; summarize information from different sources

items: A1 (Beginner): Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions
A2 (Elementary): Can communicate in simple and routine tasks
B1 (Intermediate): Can deal with most situations while traveling; can produce simple connected text
B2 (Upper Intermediate): Can interact with fluency; can produce clear, detailed text on various subjects
C1 (Advanced): Can express ideas fluently and spontaneously; can produce well-structured, detailed text
Primary (Years 1-6): A1-B1 acceptable with Tier 1-2 EAL support
Lower Secondary (Years 7-8): A2-B2; students below A2 need intensive Tier 3 support
IGCSE (Years 9-10): B1 minimum; B2 preferred because of the academic language demands
A Level (Years 11-12): B2 minimum; C1 preferred for essay writing and analysis
Assess number fluency, problem-solving, and understanding of concepts
Find gaps from the previous curriculum (especially for students moving from Indonesian national schools to Cambridge)
content.title: Mathematics Assessment

items: Number sense and operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division)
Fractions and decimals
Measurement and geometry basics
Simple word problems
Algebraic expressions and equations
Ratio, proportion, percentages
Geometry (angles, area, volume)
Data interpretation (graphs, charts)
Algebra (linear equations, quadratic equations, simultaneous equations)
Trigonometry and coordinate geometry
Statistics and probability
Advanced algebra (functions, logarithms, exponential)
Calculus (differentiation, integration)
Mechanics and statistics (depending on pathway)

content.text: Language Consideration: Give mathematics assessments in both English and Bahasa Indonesia to students with limited English proficiency. This way you test math ability, not just language comprehension. Other Subject Screening (for Mid-Year or Transfer Students) For students joining Year 9 (IGCSE) or Year 11 (A Level) mid-course:

items: Check what the student already knows in the chosen subjects (e.g., Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Business, Geography)
Compare the previous course content with the Cambridge syllabus requirements
Find the topics where the student needs catch-up teaching

content.text: Example: A student who transfers in Year 10 from the Indonesian national curriculum may have strong biology knowledge. But Cambridge practical skills and exam techniques can be new to them. Plan focused bridging support. Accommodations for SEN Students During Testing To assess SEN students' abilities fairly:

items: Extended time (e.g., 25% or 50% extra time)
Quiet, distraction-free testing environment
Use of assistive technology (e.g., text-to-speech software, calculator)
Breaks during longer assessments
A scribe (a person who writes for the student) for students with writing difficulties
Large print or colored overlays for students with visual processing needs

content.text: Record every accommodation given during placement testing. This record helps the school plan the student's future IEP (see 8.5.3). Results Interpretation and Communication to Parents Placement Test Report Should Include:

items: Overall performance summary (strengths and areas for growth)
CEFR level for English (if applicable)
Recommended year level placement
Suggested support services (EAL, learning support, subject tutoring)
Baseline data for tracking progress later

content.text: Sample Parent Communication: Based on [Student Name]'s placement assessments, we recommend enrollment in Year 7 with Tier 2 EAL support. [He/She] demonstrates strong mathematical reasoning and problem-solving skills. In English, [he/she] is currently at CEFR A2 level (elementary), which means [he/she] can communicate in simple, routine tasks but will need scaffolding for academic language. We will provide small-group EAL sessions three times per week, alongside in-class differentiation. We expect [Student Name] to reach B1 level (intermediate) within 12-18 months with consistent effort and support. Appeals Process for Placement Decisions If parents disagree with placement recommendations:

steps: Arrange a follow-up meeting with the Principal and the relevant Subject Leaders
Go through the assessment results in detail, with examples of the student's work
Discuss the parents' concerns and the reasons for the school's recommendation
Consider a trial period at the requested level, with progress monitoring

If the disagreement continues, offer an external assessment by an educational psychologist (the family pays for it). Final Authority: The Principal makes the final placement decision after consulting the Subject Leaders and the General Manager. The decision puts the student's best interest and realistic chance of success first.

content.text: Space Availability Assessment Before accepting mid-year transfers:

items: Check current class sizes against maximum capacity (Cambridge recommendation: 20-24 students per class)
Consider teacher-student ratios and workload
Check whether adding a student will lower the quality of education for current students
Priority for transfer students: siblings of current students, children of new staff members
Offer a place on the waitlist for the next academic year
Refer the family to other Eduversal Partner Schools that have places
Remain transparent: "We would love to welcome your child, but our Year 7 class is currently full. We can add your child to the waitlist and notify you if a space becomes available."

content.text: Curriculum Alignment Students who transfer from a different curriculum face challenges as they adjust: From the Indonesian National Curriculum to Cambridge:

items: More focus on critical thinking, inquiry and problem-solving (vs. rote memorization)
Increased English language demands
Different assessment formats (essays, practical exams, coursework)
More student-centered pedagogy

content.text: From Other International Curricula (IB, American, Australian):

items: Differences in subject content and in the order topics are taught
Different grading systems (e.g., IB 1-7 scale vs. Cambridge A-E grades)
Getting used to the exam-focused Cambridge approach in IGCSE and A Level
Do curriculum mapping to find gaps and overlaps
Provide bridging materials for key concepts the student missed
Set realistic expectations with families about how long adjustment takes (usually 1-2 terms)

content.text: For students transferring from other Cambridge schools:
content.title: Academic Record Evaluation and Credit Transfer

items: Accept Cambridge Checkpoint or IGCSE results directly
Continue coursework and exam preparation without disruption
Check transcripts against Cambridge syllabus requirements
Decide the matching year level (this may not always match the student's age)
Decide which subjects can count for credit and which the student needs to take again

content.text: Example: A Year 10 student moves from IB MYP and has a strong science background. This student may enter IGCSE Science without problems. But the student may need to catch up on some Cambridge Physics or Chemistry content. Credit Transfer Policy:

items: No automatic credit transfer for non-Cambridge qualifications
The Principal and Subject Leaders look at each case one by one
The final decision is based on the student's best interest and real chance of success in Cambridge exams

content.text:
For transfer students with gaps in what they have learned:

1. Diagnostic Assessment:
content.title: Catch-Up Support Planning

items: Give placement tests (as in Section 11.3)
Find the specific topics or skills that need more work

content.text: 2. Individualized Catch-Up Plan: - Written by Subject Leaders and the Homeroom Teacher - Lists the topics to cover, the resources to use and a timeline for finishing - May include: after-school tutoring, weekend catch-up sessions, online resources, peer tutoring 3. Progress Monitoring: - Weekly check-ins during the first term - Change the support based on the student's progress - Involve parents in practice and support at home 4. Realistic Timeline: - Full alignment with the curriculum may take 6-12 months - Some gaps in content may remain; focus on the most important basics. Important: Do not overload transfer students with too much catch-up work. Put essential content first. Give the student time to adjust socially and emotionally.

content.title: Transition Support for Transfer Students
content.text: Changing schools in the middle of the year is hard for a student, socially and emotionally:

content.title: Social Integration Strategies
items: Assign a peer buddy for the first 2-4 weeks
Introduce the student to classmates and help them feel included
Encourage the student to join extracurricular activities and clubs
Watch for signs of loneliness, anxiety, or being left out

content.title: Homeroom Teacher Role
items: Check in every day in the first week, then every week
Build rapport and trust
Talk with parents regularly about how the student is settling in
Refer the student to the school counselor if needed (see Section 9 for wellbeing support)

content.title: Parents' Role
items: Maintain open communication with school
Repeat positive messages about the new school
Arrange playdates or other social contact outside school
Be patient while the child adjusts (this usually takes 4-8 weeks)

content.text: With Parent Permission: Contact the previous school to ask for:
content.title: Communication with Previous School

items: Official transcripts and academic records
Teacher recommendations and subject reports
Disciplinary records (if any)
IEP or learning support documentation
Any safeguarding concerns or incidents

content.text: Confidentiality: Information from the previous school is used for one purpose: to support the student's move to the new school. It should be handled in line with the data protection guidelines (see Section 14). If the Previous School Does Not Respond:

items: Keep a record of each attempt to contact the school (emails, phone calls)
Continue with enrollment using the information the parents gave
Watch the student closely during the first term, which is a probation period
Watch for any differences between what the parents said and the student's actual performance/behavior

content.text:
Honesty and Accuracy in All Marketing Materials: Promotional content includes websites, brochures, social media posts and advertisements. Eduversal Partner Schools must make sure that all promotional content gives an accurate picture of:

1. Facilities and Resources:
content.title: Truth in Advertising

items: Show the school's real facilities, not ideal images from other schools
If you use stock photos, label them clearly as illustrations
Do not exaggerate (e.g., do not call a small library a "world-class media center")
State clearly which Cambridge programs the school offers (Primary, Lower Secondary, IGCSE, AS/A Level)
Say which subjects are available (do not list subjects the school does not teach now)
Describe teacher qualifications and experience accurately
Report Cambridge exam results accurately (percentage of A-C grades, pass rates, average scores)
Do not pick out only the top performers
Give context (e.g., "Out of 30 students, 25 achieved A-B grades in IGCSE Mathematics")
Celebrate achievements without misleading comparisons (e.g., do not claim "best in Indonesia" without data that can be checked)
List the real universities that have accepted former students
Do not suggest that university admission is guaranteed
Be honest about the range of places where students go (local Indonesian universities, regional, international)

content.title: No Misleading Claims About Cambridge Affiliation
Permissible Statements
items: "We are a Cambridge International School with Centre number ID123"
"Our students take Cambridge IGCSE and A Level examinations"
"We follow the Cambridge International curriculum"

content.title: Prohibited Statements
items: "We are a Cambridge University-affiliated school" (this suggests a link to the University of Cambridge, which is false)
"Cambridge-certified school" (this certification does not exist)

"Officially recognized by Cambridge University" (Cambridge International is part of the University of Cambridge. But a registered Cambridge Centre has no formal link with the University itself, and the University does not endorse it)

content.text: Compliance: Follow Cambridge International's guidelines on branding and logo use. Do not misuse the Cambridge logo or trademarks.

content.title: Honest Communication About School Stage of Development

items: Be open about how long the school has been running
Say which year groups are still growing (e.g., "We currently offer Years 1-8 and will expand to Year 9 in August 2026")
Do not claim a track record the school does not have yet. For example, do not advertise "proven success in A Levels" if no students have finished A Levels yet.
Share past data (e.g., "In our 10 years of operation, 95% of our students have been accepted to universities worldwide")
Show improvements over time (e.g., "Our IGCSE A-C pass rate has increased from 70% in 2020 to 85% in 2025")
It is fine to share the school's vision and future plans (e.g., "We aim to open a STEAM Innovation Lab in 2027")
Make clear what is true now and what is a future goal (e.g., "While we are working toward CIS accreditation, we are not yet accredited")
Law No. 8/1999 on Consumer Protection: Prohibits false or misleading advertising
Indonesian Broadcasting Commission (KPI) guidelines (if advertising on TV/radio)
Ministry of Education regulations on educational institution advertising

content.title: Key Principles
items: Do not make claims that cannot be proved
Give clear information that is easy to understand (avoid jargon)
Do not exploit children in advertising (e.g., do not use emotional appeals that manipulate people)

content.text: Written Parental Consent for Photos and Videos Before you use any student images:
content.title: Use of Student Images and Work

items: Get signed consent from parents (this is in the enrollment packet, see Section 11.4)
School website and social media
Printed brochures and promotional materials
Internal school publications (yearbook, newsletter)
Media interviews or press coverage
Parents may say no to use in external marketing and still allow internal classroom use
Consent may be withdrawn at any time
Images will not be sold to third parties
Student names will not appear next to photos unless parents give separate consent

content.text: Safeguarding Consideration: NEVER publish students' full names next to their photos in materials the public can see (e.g., on the website). Use first names only or no names at all, to protect student privacy. Student Privacy Protection Best Practices:

items: Avoid close-ups of a full face; use group photos when you can
Do not publish sensitive personal information (home address, phone number, detailed family background)
If you show student work, remove any information that could identify the student (unless consent has been given)
Store all media files safely, with controls on who can open them (see Section 14)

content.text: Age-Appropriate Representation Make sure marketing materials are diverse and inclusive:

items: Show students of different ages, genders, ethnicities, and abilities
Avoid tokenism (e.g., do not show only one student with a disability just to look inclusive)
Show students in real learning situations (not too posed or staged)
Avoid stereotypes (e.g., only boys in science labs, only girls in art classes)
Respect Islamic dress codes in photos (e.g., make sure female students wear the hijab if this is required)
Show Islamic values and practices (prayer times, Quranic studies, Ramadan observance)
Avoid images that go against Islamic principles (e.g., physical contact between boys and girls in PE classes if this is not permitted)
Be careful about cultural norms on modesty and proper behavior
Celebrate diversity while respecting religious and cultural practices
Avoid religious or political messages that may push families away

content.text: Website and Social Media Current and Accurate Information School website must include:

items: Up-to-date academic calendar
Current tuition and fee schedule
Staff directory with photos and qualifications
Curriculum overview and subject offerings
Admissions process and application forms (downloadable)
Contact information (phone, email, address, map)
Policies and handbooks (Student-Parent Handbook, Admissions Policy)
Critical information (calendar, fees): reviewed every three months
News and events: updated every week or when events happen
Staff directory: updated at once when there are staff changes

content.text: Regular Updates Social Media Best Practices:

items: Post regularly (at least 2-3 times per week) to keep followers interested
Share different kinds of content: student achievements, classroom activities, staff spotlights, event photos
Celebrate festivals and national holidays (Indonesian Independence Day, Eid, Christmas, etc.)
Encourage respectful interaction; check and manage comments to stop bullying or inappropriate content
Plan posts in advance around key school events (admissions open days, exam results, sports day, cultural festivals)
Balance promotional content with real stories of student learning and growth

content.text: Bilingual Content (English and Bahasa Indonesia) Accessibility Requirement:

items: All critical information (admissions, tuition, policies) must be available in both languages
Use professional translation, not Google Translate
Make sure the English and Bahasa Indonesia versions say the same thing
May switch between languages (some posts in English, others in Bahasa Indonesia)
For important announcements, post in both languages or give a translation in the comments

content.text: Rationale: Eduversal Partner Schools serve many different families. Some are more comfortable in Bahasa Indonesia, and some prefer English. Accessibility Features Website Accessibility (compliance with WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines):

items: Text size adjustable
High contrast mode for visually impaired users
Alt text for all images (describe images for screen readers)
Keyboard navigation (for users unable to use a mouse)
Captions or transcripts for video content
Make sure the website works well on phones (many parents look for information on smartphones)
Test the website on different devices and browsers

content.title: Website Privacy Policy
items: Clearly state how user data is collected, stored, and used
Give users a way to opt out of cookies or tracking
Link to full Data Protection Policy (see Section 14)

content.title: Secure Forms
items: Use SSL encryption for online application or inquiry forms
Do not ask for sensitive information (e.g., bank account details) through channels that are not secure

content.text: Compliance: Act in line with Indonesian data protection norms and UU No. 27/2022 (Personal Data Protection Law). Use GDPR as a best-practice comparison.

content.title: Transparent Fee Structure
content.text: When Discussing Tuition with Prospective Parents:

items: Give a full breakdown of costs (tuition, enrollment fee, development fee, extra expenses)
Be open from the start about possible extra costs (uniforms, trips, exam fees)
Explain what tuition includes (meals, textbooks, extracurriculars)
Explain payment schedules and installment options

content.text: Avoid Hidden Fees: Do not surprise families with unexpected charges after enrollment.

items: Explain how the placement assessment works and why the school uses it
Be realistic about academic expectations (e.g., "Cambridge curriculum is rigorous; students should be prepared to work hard and manage challenging content")
Explain what EAL (English as an Additional Language) and SEN (Special Educational Needs) support is available, and its limits
Describe the typical student (e.g., "Most of our students come from Indonesian national schools and are EAL learners; we provide strong language support")

content.text: Do Not Overpromise: If the school cannot guarantee a place (e.g., because of limited space), say so from the start.

content.title: Honest Discussion of Student Support Services

items: EAL pull-out sessions (small-group work outside the class) and in-class scaffolding (step-by-step support)
Learning support for students with mild-to-moderate SEN
Counseling and pastoral care
Academic tutoring (if offered)
We do not provide specialized therapy (speech, occupational, behavioral)
We cannot support students with severe developmental disabilities who need a 1-on-1 aide
Our EAL support helps students build their English, but becoming fluent takes 1-3 years
Learning support is given in groups, not individually (unless an IEP requires it)

content.text: Transparency Builds Trust: Families value honesty. They are more likely to enroll if expectations are clear from the start.

content.title: No Pressure Tactics or False Urgency
Unethical Practices to Avoid
items: "Only 2 spots left! Enroll today or lose your chance!" (unless it is really true)
"Special discount only if you sign up this week" (made-up deadlines to pressure families)
"Other schools are inferior; we are the only good choice" (speaking badly of other schools)
Very pushy follow-up calls or messages after the first inquiry

content.title: Ethical Enrollment Practices
items: Give accurate information about how many places are available
Give families time to make informed decisions
Respect parents' choice to visit multiple schools before deciding
Follow up politely and professionally, without putting pressure on families

content.title: After Initial Inquiry
items: Send welcome email with key information (admissions process, tuition, school calendar)
Invite the family to book a school tour or open house
Give a contact person for further questions (Admissions Coordinator, Principal)

content.title: After School Visit
items: Send thank-you email
Offer to answer extra questions
Give the application form and a checklist of required documents
Set a clear timeline for the next steps

content.title: If Family Has Not Responded
items: Send one polite follow-up reminder (1-2 weeks after the first contact)
If a family stops replying, accept that they might not be interested. Do not harass them.
Keep the family on the general mailing list for newsletters and event invitations, with an option to opt out

content.title: Record-Keeping
items: Keep a record of all contact with prospective families in a CRM (customer relationship management) system or spreadsheet
Track inquiries, visits, applications, and enrollment decisions
Use the data to judge how well each marketing strategy works

content.title: When to Use Waitlists
items: Classes are full, but places might open up because students withdraw or transfer
The school wants to keep qualified applicants interested for future enrollment
Mid-year or late applications for popular year levels (for example, Year 7 or Year 9)
Tell the family that the student is on the waitlist and has not been rejected
Explain: "We are unable to offer a spot at this time due to capacity constraints, but we would like to keep your application active in case a space becomes available."
Date of application (first-come, first-served)
Sibling enrollment (priority for families who are already part of the school community)
Matching specific needs (for example, a student whose subject interests fit the places available)
Contact waitlisted families every month (or every quarter)
Give realistic expectations: "We typically see 2-3 openings per year in Year 8 due to family relocations."
If no place becomes available, offer the family the option to stay on the waitlist for the next academic year
Contact the family immediately when a place becomes available
Give the family 3-5 business days to accept the offer
If the family declines, offer the place to the next person on the waitlist

content.text: Transparency: Families want to know clearly where they are on the waitlist and how likely they are to be admitted.

In order of priority:

1. Siblings of Currently Enrolled Students:
content.title: Priority Criteria for Waitlist Movement

items: The family is already committed to the school community
Simplifies logistics for family

content.text: 2. Students with Specific Skill or Background Needed:

items: Example: there is a waitlist for Year 11 A Level and a place opens in the Physics class. Give priority to a student with a strong science background.
Among applicants with similar qualifications: first come, first served
The student urgently needs to transfer because of bullying, school closure or family relocation

content.text: Important: Waitlist priority should NOT include:

items: Ability to pay full tuition (no "buying" a spot)
Family connections or donations (unless there is a transparent, board-approved development policy)

content.text: When Schools May Reject Applications: Legitimate Reasons:
content.title: Appeals Process for Rejected Applications

items: The student needs more support than the school can give — for example, severe SEN (special educational needs) that need a 1-on-1 aide
Significant behavioral or disciplinary concerns from the previous school that suggest the student would be unsafe or disruptive
No space in the requested year level, and no places expected to open
Student's religion, ethnicity, gender, or disability (see Section 11.2 for non-discrimination policy)
Family's socioeconomic status or inability to pay full tuition
The student's EAL (English as an Additional Language) status or limited English proficiency

content.text: Appeal Process: Step 1: Written Appeal Submission

content.title: Admissions Appeal Record — Documentation, Review Meeting, Evidence Considered
rows: Additional Evidence Considered — Updated medical reports
Additional Evidence Considered — Teacher recommendation letters
Additional Evidence Considered — Improved test scores

items: Parents send a written appeal to the Principal within 14 days of being told about the rejection
The appeal must explain why the parents disagree with the decision
Include any extra documents or evidence that the school did not consider before (for example, updated medical reports, recommendation letters, proof of progress)
Principal and relevant staff (Subject Leaders, Learning Support Coordinator) review appeal
Arrange a meeting with the parents to discuss the concerns
Consider extra assessment or trial period if appropriate
The Principal makes the final decision after consulting the General Manager
Tell the parents the decision in writing within 10 business days
If the appeal succeeds, continue with enrollment
If the appeal is denied, explain the reasons clearly and suggest other options (other schools, or applying again next year)
If parents believe the decision was discriminatory or unfair, they may appeal to the Yayasan Board
The Board carries out an independent review and makes a binding decision
First rejection notice: sent within 1 week of the application review
Parent appeal submission: within 14 days of rejection
School appeal review and response: within 10 business days
Total appeals process: about 3-4 weeks
content.title: Timeline for Appeals Review

content.text: Expedited Appeals: In urgent cases, the school may review the appeal faster. For example, a student needs a place immediately because their previous school closed.

content.title: Principal's Role
items: Makes day-to-day admissions decisions for standard applications
Has authority to accept, reject, or waitlist applicants

content.title: General Manager's Role
items: Is consulted on appeals, unusual cases, or policy exceptions
Makes sure decisions follow Eduversal standards and Yayasan policies

content.title: Yayasan Board's Role
items: Acts as the final external review in disputed cases
Makes sure the school follows non-discrimination and ethical principles
Does not interfere with routine admissions decisions

content.text: Principle: Educational professionals (Principal, teachers) should make admissions decisions based on the student's best interest, not because of outside pressure.

content.title: Parent Responsibilities
items: Parents must give written notice (email or letter) to the Principal and the Finance Office at least 1 month before the planned withdrawal date
The notice period lets the school manage class sizes and plan to fill the place
If parents do not give enough notice, they lose one month's tuition (the "in lieu of notice" clause in the enrollment contract)

content.title: Example
items: A parent gives withdrawal notice on October 15 and says the student will leave on November 20
The school charges tuition for all of November (even though the student leaves in the middle of the month)
A parent gives notice on October 15 but wants the student to leave immediately (October 15). In this case, the school charges full November tuition as a penalty.

content.title: Exceptions to Notice Requirement
items: Emergencies (serious family illness, sudden relocation)
Withdrawal started by the school (disciplinary expulsion — rare and only after due process, see Section 22)

content.title: Purpose of Exit Interview
items: Understand why the family is leaving (feedback to help the school improve)
Make the move smooth for the student and family
Keep a good relationship (families may come back or recommend the school to others)
Deal with any open issues or concerns

content.title: Interview Conducted by
items: Principal or Admissions Coordinator
In-person, phone, or video call (as the family prefers)

content.title: Reason for Withdrawal
items: Family relocation
Financial constraints
Academic fit (curriculum too hard or not hard enough)
Social or behavioral concerns (bullying, peer conflicts)
Unhappiness with teaching, communication, or school policies
Logistical challenges (transportation, schedule)

content.title: Overall School Experience
items: What did your family appreciate most about our school?
What areas could we improve?
How would you describe your child's academic progress and social experience?
Did you feel supported by teachers and administration?

content.title: Future Plans
items: Where is your child enrolling next?
Can we assist with records transfer or recommendations?

content.title: Would You Recommend Our School?
items: Net Promoter Score (NPS): "On a scale of 0-10, how likely are you to recommend our school to another family?"

content.title: Document Exit Interview
items: Write the main feedback in a confidential summary
Share common themes with the Senior Leadership Team to keep improving
Track the reasons for withdrawal over time. If several families leave for the same reason, find out the root causes.

content.title: Student Records Transfer
content.text: **School's Responsibility:** When a family makes a formal withdrawal request, the school must provide:

content.title: Official Transcript
items: All grades and academic records from the student's time at the school
Signed and stamped by Principal
Given in a sealed envelope (to protect their integrity)

content.title: Transfer Letter or School Leaving Certificate
items: Confirms student was enrolled from [start date] to [end date]
States year level completed
States that the student left in good standing (unless there were disciplinary issues)

content.title: Attendance Records
items: Summary of attendance and punctuality

content.title: Copy of Student Records
items: For parent's personal records
Includes: report cards, standardized test scores (Cambridge Checkpoint, EASE) and IEP/ILP documents (Individual Education Plan / Individual Learning Plan), if applicable

content.title: Recommendation Letter (Optional)
items: If parents ask for it for an application to a new school
Highlight student's strengths, contributions, and character
Be honest but helpful. Avoid comments that are too negative.

content.title: Timeline
items: Provide records within 5-10 business days of written request
Send them faster if it is urgent (the student is starting at a new school immediately)

content.title: Records Retention
items: The school keeps copies of student records for the periods set in the combined retention schedule in Section 14.5. The admissions summary is in 11.9. The period is different for each type of record.

content.title: Release of Records to New School
items: Only with written parental authorization
Send them directly to the new school's admissions office, not to the parents, to protect their integrity

content.title: Exit Interview Template — Key Questions
rows: What did family appreciate most about our school?
Would family recommend school to others?

content.title: Exit Interview Template — Identification, Reason for Withdrawal, Experience Rating
rows: Overall Experience Rating — 1 (Very Dissatisfied) to 5 (Very Satisfied)

content.title: Final Report Card
items: Provide the latest term report (or a mid-term progress report if the student leaves in the middle of a term)
Include teacher comments and attendance summary

content.title: Certificates to Provide
items: Cambridge Checkpoint Statements of Achievement (if student completed Grade 6 or Grade 8)
IGCSE or A Level certificates (if exams completed)
Participation certificates for extracurricular activities, sports, or competitions
Character or service awards earned during enrollment

content.text: Make sure every certificate is signed, dated and carries the official school seal.

content.title: Refund Policy Application
content.text: See the Enrollment Contract and Section 11.4 for the full refund policy:

content.title: Tuition Refund
items: Calculated on a pro-rata basis for the part of the term not used
If a student withdraws in October, the school refunds November-June tuition (if it was paid in advance)
Deduct one month's tuition if the family did not give the full notice period

content.title: Non-Refundable Fees
items: Enrollment fee
Development fee
Exam fees (if the student is already registered with Cambridge)

content.title: Refund Processing Timeline
items: Refunds are processed within 30 days after the withdrawal is confirmed
Paid by bank transfer or check to the parent's account

content.title: Outstanding Balances
items: The school pursues unpaid tuition, fees, or fines through a structured payment plan, late fees, or suspension of optional services
Academic records, transcripts, report cards, diplomas, and certificates are NEVER withheld for non-payment. Results of exams the student has already sat are never blocked either (see 2.9).

content.title: Maintaining Alumni Relationships
items: All students who complete at least one full year at the school are considered alumni
Invite alumni to join school alumni network (email list, WhatsApp group, LinkedIn group)
Encourage alumni to stay connected and return for school events

content.title: Alumni Benefits
items: Invitations to annual alumni gathering or reunion
The chance to join the alumni mentorship program (alumni mentor current students)
Priority enrollment for siblings or children of alumni
Networking opportunities with other alumni

content.title: Alumni Database
items: Keep alumni contact details (with their consent) to stay in touch with them
Track which universities alumni go to and their career paths
Celebrate alumni achievements in school newsletters and social media

content.text: Goodwill Message: "Even though your child is leaving, they will always be part of our school family. We wish them every success and hope they will stay in touch."

content.text: Data Protection Practices. UU No. 27/2022 concerning Personal Data Protection (Pelindungan Data Pribadi, "UU PDP") governs how admissions data is handled. It was enacted on 17 October 2022 and has been fully in force since 17 October 2024. Section 14 is the controlling text for this manual. The principles below carry out UU PDP. GDPR is mentioned only as an international best practice for comparison:

content.title: Lawfulness, Fairness, and Transparency
items: Data collection has legitimate educational purpose
Parents are informed about what data is collected and why
Privacy policies are written in clear, easy-to-understand language

content.title: Purpose Limitation
items: Student data used only for stated purposes (education, assessment, safety)
Not sold or shared with third parties for marketing

content.title: Data Minimization
items: Collect only the data needed for educational work
Do not ask for too much information, or for information that is not relevant

content.title: Accuracy
items: Maintain up-to-date student records
Let parents check and correct mistakes

content.title: Storage Limitation
items: Keep student records only for as long as legally required or educationally necessary
Delete data securely after the retention period ends (see the records retention schedule below)

content.title: Integrity and Confidentiality
items: Protect student data with appropriate security measures
Allow access to authorized staff only

content.title: Accountability
items: The school is responsible for showing that it follows data protection principles
Regular audits and Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs)

content.title: Student Data Security in the Admissions Process
Personal Information
items: Student name, date of birth, gender, nationality
Home address, contact information
Parent names, occupations, contact details
Previous schools attended
NISN (for Indonesian students)

content.title: Sensitive Information
items: Health records and medical conditions
Learning support needs and psychological assessments
Behavioral or disciplinary records
Financial information (for scholarship applications)

content.title: Physical Security
items: Admissions files are kept in locked cabinets in a secure office
Access is limited to the Admissions Coordinator, the Principal and authorized administrative staff

content.title: Digital Security
items: Student data is stored in a password-protected database (EduNav or the school management system)
Multi-factor authentication for admin users
Regular backups to secure server
Sensitive documents are sent in encrypted form (for example, through a secure portal, not regular email)

content.text: **Best Practice:** Do NOT send student medical records, psychological assessments or financial documents by unencrypted email. Use secure file-sharing platforms (Google Drive with restricted access, password-protected attachments) or collect the documents in person.

Required Consents (obtained during enrollment, see Section 11.4):

1. General Data Processing:
content.title: Parent Consent for Data Use

items: Storage and use of student information for educational, administrative, and safety purposes

The consent form should specify: "We will collect and store your child's personal information (name, date of birth, academic records, health information) to provide quality education, ensure safety, and comply with legal requirements."

items.text: Name the outside organizations that will receive student data:
items: Cambridge International (exam registration)
Indonesian Ministry of Education (Dapodik reporting)
Accreditation bodies (CIS, WASC) during site visits
Insurance companies (for student accident insurance)
Educational service providers (e.g., school bus company, field trip organizers)
Get separate consent for each category, or give opt-out options
Separate consent for marketing and promotional use (see Section 11.6)
Right to see their child's data (ask for a copy of the student file)
Right to correct mistakes (update contact information, medical records)
Right to limit processing (opt out of data uses that are not essential)
Right to withdraw consent (for example, take back photo consent at any time)
Right to data portability (to receive student records in a format that can be moved to another system)

content.title: How Long to Keep Student Records
Active Students
items: All records are kept in the current student file
Updated every year (new report cards, health forms, etc.)

content.title: Student Record Retention Periods After Departure
rows: May be needed for future university applications or employment verification
Enrollment + 5 years after resolution or graduation (whichever is later)
Indonesian student rights regulations; appeals period (per 14.5)
Enrollment + 3 years after graduation (accepted students); 1 year after decision (declined applicants)
Admissions policy; audit trail; data minimization (per 14.5)
Educational records may be needed for adult services or disability support

content.title: Secure Disposal After Retention Period
items: Physical records: shredding
Digital records: secure deletion with data-wiping software (not just "delete")

content.text: Storage Location: Archived student records are kept in a secure, climate-controlled facility (off-site or a locked storage room). Access is restricted.

Organizations with a Legitimate Right to See Student Data:

1. Cambridge Assessment International Education:
content.title: Third-Party Data Sharing

items: Purpose: Exam registration, results processing
Data shared: Student name, date of birth, exam entries, candidate numbers
Compliance: Cambridge's own data protection policies apply
Purpose: Dapodik (national student database) reporting
Data shared: Student demographics, enrollment status, attendance, NISN
Compliance: Indonesian Law No. 20/2003 on National Education System
Purpose: School evaluation and accreditation site visits
Data shared: Student work samples, assessment data, demographics (anonymized when possible)
Compliance: CIS and WASC confidentiality agreements
Purpose: Student accident or health insurance coverage
Data shared: Student name, date of birth, school enrollment status
Compliance: Insurance provider's data protection policies
Purpose: School trips, transportation, catering, online learning platforms
Data shared: the smallest amount of information needed to deliver the service
Compliance: Data processing agreements with vendors (they set out confidentiality, security measures, and no use of the data for any other purpose)

content.text: **Important:** Do NOT share student data with vendors for marketing. For example, do not give student email lists to tutoring companies, even if they offer commissions.

content.title: Incident Response
content.text: If there is a data breach (unauthorized access to, loss of, or theft of student data):

content.title: Immediate Actions
items: Secure the affected systems (shut down the affected server, change passwords)
Find out how big the breach is (how many records are affected and what data was exposed)
Contain the breach to stop further damage

content.title: Notification
items: Tell the affected people (data subjects) and the supervisory authority within 3x24 hours, as required by UU No. 27/2022 Article 46(1)
Report to the Yayasan Board and Eduversal management

content.title: Remediation

content.text:
Penerimaan Peserta Didik Baru (PPDB) Compliance Indonesian Ministry of Education Regulation on Student Admissions: Key Requirements (per Permendikbudristek on PPDB):

1. Non-Discrimination:
content.title: Indonesian Requirements

items: Schools may not refuse admission based on religion, ethnicity, gender, disability, or socioeconomic status
Private schools (including Eduversal Partner Schools) have more flexibility than public schools. They must still follow equity principles.
Entry to Grade 1 (Primary): minimum age 6 years (by July 1 of the enrollment year)
Entry to Grade 7 (Secondary): maximum age 15 years
Entry to Grade 10 (High School): maximum age 18 years
Admission criteria must be available to the public (on the school website, in brochures)
Selection process must be objective, accountable, and free from corruption
Public schools give priority to students from the local catchment area
Private schools are not bound by zoning. They may give priority to the local community to make access easier.
National PPDB period: usually May-June for the August intake
Schools should match their admissions cycle to the national timeline (private schools have more flexibility)
Publish admissions policy on website in Bahasa Indonesia
Form a PPDB Committee (Panitia PPDB) with clear roles (Principal, Admissions Coordinator, Subject Leaders)
Record each admissions decision and the reason for it (especially rejections)
Report new student enrollments to the local Education Office (Dinas Pendidikan)

content.text: NISN (Nomor Induk Siswa Nasional) is the unique national student identification number. When to Register for NISN:
content.title: NISN Registration Process

items: All students enrolled in Indonesian schools (public or private) must have an NISN
An NISN is requested for each new student within 30 days of enrollment
Students who transfer from other Indonesian schools already have an NISN (the school asks the previous school to transfer it)

content.text:
Registration Process:

1. Collect Required Documents: the student's Akta Kelahiran (birth certificate), the Kartu Keluarga (family card), and the completed NISN application form.

2. Submit to Dapodik: The school's Dapodik operator enters the student data into the system. The system creates the NISN automatically (if the student is new to the Indonesian education system). Check that the NISN is correct and link it to the student profile.

3. NISN Verification: Check the NISN status on the official portal (https://nisn.data.kemdikbud.go.id/). Make sure the NISN is active and correctly linked to the school.

4. Update NISN Annually: Each semester, check that all student NISN records in Dapodik are up to date. Update a record if a student changes name, year level, or status. International Students:

items: Students who are not Indonesian citizens and do not plan to go on to Indonesian higher education may be exempt from NISN
However, if international students study in Indonesia for a long time, NISN registration is recommended so their records continue without a break

content.text: For more details on Dapodik compliance, see Section 2.4.

content.title: Dapodik Data Entry for New Students
content.text: Dapodik (Data Pokok Pendidikan) is the Indonesian Ministry's national education database:

content.title: Student Demographics
items: Full name, NISN, date of birth, gender
Nationality, religion
Home address, parent/guardian contact information

content.title: Enrollment Status
items: School entry date, current year level
Homeroom teacher assignment
Boarding or day student status

content.title: Academic Records
items: Previous school name and NPSN (if applicable)
Grades and attendance (updated each semester)

content.title: Timeline
items: New student data must be entered within 30 days of enrollment
Dapodik is updated on the Ministry’s synchronization calendar — see 14.7

content.text: **Compliance Check:** The Principal and the Dapodik operator should carry out a quarterly audit. It checks that all enrolled students are recorded correctly in Dapodik.

content.title: BAN-S/M Admissions Standards
content.text: BAN-S/M (Badan Akreditasi Nasional Sekolah/Madrasah) is Indonesia's national school accreditation body:

content.title: Standard 1: Admissions and Capacity
items: The school has a clear, written admissions policy
Admissions process is transparent, accountable, and non-discriminatory
Class sizes are appropriate (maximum 28-32 students per class)
Teacher-student ratios meet national standards (1:20 for primary, 1:24 for secondary)

content.title: Standard 2: Documentation
items: Student files are complete (birth certificate, previous school reports, health records)
Enrollment contracts are signed and stored securely
Admissions records are organized and accessible for audit

content.title: Standard 3: Equity and Inclusion
items: The school is open to students of different backgrounds and abilities
Scholarship or financial aid opportunities are available (if possible)
Students with SEN (special educational needs) get appropriate support

content.title: Evidence for BAN-S/M Accreditation Visit
items: Admissions Policy document (in Bahasa Indonesia)
Sample application forms and enrollment contracts
Records of admissions decisions (anonymized)
Statistics: number of applicants, acceptance rate, demographic diversity
Documentation of SEN support and accommodations provided

content.title: Centre Registration of Candidates
content.text: **Cambridge Exam Registration Requirements:** Schools must register students (candidates) for Cambridge exams by the published deadlines:

content.title: Entry Deadlines (approximate)
items: March Series (if offered): October of the previous year
June Series: February
November Series: see the key dates table in Section 10

content.title: Collect Candidate Information
items: Full legal name (as on passport or birth certificate)
Date of birth
Gender
Candidate number (given by the school; numbered in sequence)

content.title: Enter Data into Cambridge Portal
items: The Exams Officer logs in to the Cambridge International Direct portal
Enters candidate details and exam entries (subjects, components)
Checks for mistakes (name spelling, date of birth, subject codes)

content.title: Pay Exam Fees
items: Calculate the total fees (Cambridge charges a fee for each subject for each candidate)
Submit payment to Cambridge by the deadline
Late entries incur extra fees

content.title: Verify Entries
items: Cambridge sends confirmation statement
Cross-check against school records
Report discrepancies immediately to Cambridge

content.title: Admissions Implication
items: Students who join Year 10 (IGCSE) or Year 12 (AS Level) in the middle of the year may miss exam registration deadlines
Schools must inform families: "If your child enrolls after [date], they may not be able to sit exams in June and will need to wait until November series or following year."

content.title: Accurate Candidate Information
content.text: Cambridge requires precise personal information for exam certificates:

content.title: Critical Data
items: Legal name (as it will appear on certificate)
Date of birth (used to check age and for special consideration requests)
Gender (for statistical reporting; use "other" if preferred)

content.title: Common Errors to Avoid
items: Misspelled names (check against official documents)
Incorrect date of birth (can cause problems with university applications)
Inconsistent name formatting (e.g., "Muhammad Ali" vs. "Muhamad Ali")

content.text: Best Practice: During admissions, collect a photocopy of the passport or birth certificate. Use it as the definitive source for Cambridge registration.
Admissions Cycle Must Consider Cambridge Timelines: For New Year 10 Students (IGCSE):
content.title: Timeline Alignment with Exam Registration Deadlines

items: Ideally, students enroll before February so they can be registered for June exams (for subjects taken in Year 10, if applicable)

If a student enrolls after the June-series entry deadline (about February), they may face late entry fees or be unable to enter that series. Year 10 is still the IGCSE examination year. The Exams Officer confirms the next available series.

content.text: For New Year 11 Students (AS Level study year):

items: There are no Cambridge examination entries in Year 11. Students sit AS Level examinations in the Year 12 October/November series.
Students who enroll late join AS Level study that has already started. AS pacing cannot be adjusted. So the school plans catch-up before the Year 12 October/November AS series.

content.text: For New Year 12 Students (AS Level; A Level for approved continuers):

items: Enroll before the Year 12 October/November AS entry deadline. Approved A Level continuers are entered for the Year 12 May/June series.
Mid-year transfers into Year 12 are extremely difficult to accommodate (students would have missed AS coursework and assessments)

content.text: Admissions Communication: Tell prospective families clearly about these limits at their first inquiry and during the application process.

content.title: CIS/WASC Standards
content.text:
**Fair and Transparent Admissions**

CIS (Council of International Schools) and WASC (Western Association of Schools and Colleges) Accreditation Standards:

content.title: Standard: Access and Equity
items: The school has a written admissions policy. It is fair and transparent, and it is applied consistently.
Admissions criteria are clearly communicated to prospective families
The school does not discriminate based on protected characteristics (race, religion, gender, disability, nationality)

content.title: Standard: Enrollment Management
items: The school keeps enrollment at a level that allows a quality education
Class sizes and teacher-student ratios support good learning
Waitlist management is ethical and transparent

content.title: Standard: Marketing Integrity
items: The school's promotional materials are accurate and not misleading
Claims about academic results, facilities, and programs are supported by evidence
The use of student images and work follows privacy and consent requirements

content.title: Evidence for CIS/WASC Accreditation
items: Admissions Policy (including non-discrimination statement)
Admissions process flowchart (from inquiry to enrollment)
Decision records (show consistency and fairness)
Marketing materials review log (approval process for brochures, website content)
Parent consent forms for photo/video use

content.title: Non-Discrimination Policies
content.text:
**Required Policy Elements:**

**Statement of Inclusion:** "[School Name] welcomes students of all backgrounds, abilities, and identities. We do not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national or ethnic origin, religion, gender, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, age, disability, or socioeconomic status in admissions or any school programs and activities."

content.title: Implementation Actions
items: Train admissions staff on unconscious bias and inclusive practices
Make sure application forms do not ask for unnecessary information that could bias decisions (e.g., parent occupation, family income)
Check admissions data for patterns of exclusion (e.g., unusually low acceptance rates for certain groups)

content.title: Grievance Mechanism
items: Give families a clear process to raise concerns about discriminatory treatment
Investigate complaints promptly and impartially
Report findings to the Yayasan Board and accreditation bodies as required

content.title: Community Engagement and Accessibility
content.text:
**CIS/WASC Standard: Community Engagement**

Schools should work actively with prospective families and the local community:

content.title: Outreach Strategies
items: Host open houses and campus tours (quarterly)
Take part in education fairs and community events
Offer presentations at feeder schools (primary schools for secondary admissions)
Invite alumni to act as ambassadors (sharing their success stories)

content.title: Accessibility Considerations
items: Make sure school facilities are accessible for families with disabilities (ramps, elevators, accessible restrooms)
Provide bilingual admissions materials (English and Bahasa Indonesia)
Offer flexible meeting times (evenings, weekends) for working parents
Consider financial aid or sliding-scale tuition (fees that change with what a family can pay) for families who cannot afford full fees

content.title: Community Partnerships
items: Work with local businesses to sponsor scholarships
Work with community organizations to find underserved students who would benefit from Cambridge education
Offer scholarships for high-achieving students from low-income backgrounds

content.title: Evidence for Accreditation
items: Records of open houses and campus tours (attendance, feedback)
Financial aid recipients (to show socioeconomic diversity)
Community partnership agreements (MOUs with sponsoring organizations)

content.title: Marketing Ethics and Truth in Advertising
content.text:
**CIS/WASC Standard: Integrity in Communications**

Schools must make sure that all marketing and communications are:

content.title: Accurate
items: Claims about facilities, programs and results can be checked
Do not exaggerate or embellish

content.title: Transparent
items: Say clearly what tuition includes and what costs extra
Be open about limitations (e.g., "We are a growing school; A Level program launches in 2027")

content.title: Ethical
items: Do not denigrate competing schools
Respect the privacy of students and families (get consent for photos and videos)
Avoid sales tactics that manipulate or pressure families

content.title: Evidence for Accreditation
items: Approval log for marketing materials (who approves content before it is published)
Website audit (check that the information is accurate)
Parent consent forms for use of student images
Complaints log (record and resolve any complaints about misleading information)
